claim: Jasmonate-deficient Nicotiana attenuata plants suffer more damage by arthropod and vertebrate herbivores than jasmonate-producing plants in nature.
source: We demonstrate that jasmonate-deficient Nicotiana attenuata plants suffer more damage by arthropod and vertebrate herbivores than jasmonate-producing plants in nature.
evidence: Supported by field observations across three experimental populations showing increased damage in irAOC plants compared to wild type plants.

claim: Only damage by vertebrate herbivores translates into a significant reduction in flower production in jasmonate-deficient plants.
source: However, only damage by vertebrate herbivores translates into a significant reduction in flower production.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis showing correlation between vertebrate damage and reduced flower production in field experiments.

claim: Vertebrate stem peeling has the strongest negative impact on plant flower production.
source: Vertebrate stem peeling has the strongest negative impact on plant flower production.
evidence: Supported by field data and glasshouse experiments showing 78% reduction in flower production following stem peeling.

claim: Stems are defended by jasmonate-dependent nicotine.
source: Stems are defended by jasmonate-dependent nicotine, and the native cottontail rabbit Sylvilagus nuttallii avoids jasmonate-producing N. attenuata shoots because of their high levels of nicotine.
evidence: Supported by metabolite profiling showing higher nicotine levels in wild type stems compared to jasmonate-deficient stems, and feeding experiments showing nicotine-dependent avoidance.

claim: The native cottontail rabbit Sylvilagus nuttallii avoids jasmonate-producing N. attenuata shoots because of their high levels of nicotine.
source: Stems are defended by jasmonate-dependent nicotine, and the native cottontail rabbit Sylvilagus nuttallii avoids jasmonate-producing N. attenuata shoots because of their high levels of nicotine.
evidence: Supported by controlled feeding experiments showing rabbits avoid wild type pellets but consume jasmonate-deficient pellets, and avoid jasmonate-deficient pellets when complemented with nicotine.

claim: Endogenous jasmonates enable plants to resist different types of herbivores in nature.
source: Thus, endogenous jasmonates enable plants to resist different types of herbivores in nature, and jasmonate-dependent defenses are important for plants to maintain their reproductive potential when facing vertebrate herbivory.
evidence: Supported by field data showing reduced damage in wild type plants compared to jasmonate-deficient plants across multiple herbivore types.

claim: Jasmonate-dependent defenses are important for plants to maintain their reproductive potential when facing vertebrate herbivory.
source: Thus, endogenous jasmonates enable plants to resist different types of herbivores in nature, and jasmonate-dependent defenses are important for plants to maintain their reproductive potential when facing vertebrate herbivory.
evidence: Supported by field data showing reduced flower production in jasmonate-deficient plants experiencing vertebrate damage.

claim: Herbivory can negatively affect plant fitness, impose selection pressure, and drive the evolution of plant defenses.
source: By removing plant tissues and interrupting essential physiological processes, herbivory can negatively affect plant fitness, impose selection pressure, and thus drive the evolution of plant defenses (Züst et al., 2012; Agrawal et al., 2012; Huber et al., 2016a; 2016b).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research on herbivory effects on plant fitness and defense evolution.

claim: Herbivory does not necessarily reduce plant survival and reproduction.
source: Herbivory does not necessarily reduce plant survival and reproduction, however (Bruelheide and Scheidel, 1999; Morris et al., 2007; Corbett et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research showing context-dependent effects of herbivory.

claim: Minor insect herbivory that occurs early in the growing season can induce plant defenses and ensure enhanced protection during times of greater herbivore abundance.
source: For example, minor insect herbivory that occurs early in the growing season can induce plant defenses, and thereby ensure enhanced protection during times of greater herbivore abundance (Agrawal, 1998; Kessler and Baldwin, 2004; Poelman et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research on induced defenses.

claim: Most plant defenses are regulated by jasmonates.
source: Most plant defenses are regulated by jasmonates (Howe and Jander, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to review article on jasmonate regulation of plant defenses.

claim: Interrupting the biosynthesis of jasmonates results in decreased constitutive and induced production of volatile and non-volatile secondary metabolites, defensive proteins and structural defenses.
source: Interrupting the biosynthesis of these hormones results in decreased constitutive and induced production of volatile and non-volatile secondary metabolites, defensive proteins and structural defenses (Thaler et al., 2002; Li et al., 2004; Paschold et al., 2007; Howe and Jander, 2008; Zhou et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research on jasmonate biosynthesis mutants.

claim: Fitness benefits of endogenous jasmonate production in herbivore-attacked plants in natural environments have not been demonstrated prior to this study.
source: Surprisingly, however, despite the availability of many different jasmonate deficient mutants (McConn et al., 1997; Thaler et al., 2002; Zhou et al., 2009; Kallenbach et al., 2012), fitness benefits of endogenous jasmonate production in herbivore-attacked plants in natural environments have not been demonstrated so far.
evidence: Supported by review of existing literature showing lack of field-based fitness studies with jasmonate mutants.

claim: Exogenous applications of jasmonic acid or methyl jasmonate enhance plant defenses and fitness.
source: Exogenous applications of jasmonic acid (JA) or methyl jasmonate (MeJA) are known to enhance plant defenses and fitness (Baldwin, 1998; Thaler, 1999; Heil et al., 2001), but these treatments remain difficult to interpret because they may not simulate dosages, localizations, and timings of endogenous jasmonate responses.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research on exogenous jasmonate applications.

claim: Exogenous jasmonate treatments are difficult to interpret because they may not simulate dosages, localizations, and timings of endogenous jasmonate responses.
source: Exogenous applications of jasmonic acid (JA) or methyl jasmonate (MeJA) are known to enhance plant defenses and fitness (Baldwin, 1998; Thaler, 1999; Heil et al., 2001), but these treatments remain difficult to interpret because they may not simulate dosages, localizations, and timings of endogenous jasmonate responses.
evidence: Based on logical inference about limitations of exogenous hormone applications.

claim: Jasmonates can reduce plant growth by interfering with gibberellin and auxin signaling cascades.
source: Apart from inducing defenses, jasmonates can also reduce plant growth (Baldwin, 1998; Hanley, 1998; Redman et al., 2001; Zavala and Baldwin, 2006; Bodenhausen and Reymond, 2007; Machado et al., 2013), by interfering, for example, with the gibberellin and auxin signaling cascades (Onkokesung et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research on jasmonate-growth trade-offs.

claim: The evolution of jasmonate defense signaling is accompanied by growth suppression that may reduce fitness benefits under low herbivore pressure.
source: This suggests that the evolution of jasmonate defense signaling is accompanied by growth suppression that may reduce fitness benefits under low herbivore pressure.
evidence: Based on inference from cited research on jasmonate-growth trade-offs.

claim: Most research on jasmonates in plant-herbivore interactions has focused on leaf-feeding arthropods.
source: Our understanding of jasmonates in plant-herbivore interactions is also wanting because most research has focused on leaf-feeding arthropods (Mafli et al., 2012; Falk et al., 2014), and much less is known with respect to vertebrate herbivores, even though vertebrates are often the primary consumers in plant communities (Paige and Whitham, 1987; Hodgson and Illius, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research and review of literature focus.

claim: Vertebrates are often the primary consumers in plant communities.
source: Our understanding of jasmonates in plant-herbivore interactions is also wanting because most research has focused on leaf-feeding arthropods (Mafli et al., 2012; Falk et al., 2014), and much less is known with respect to vertebrate herbivores, even though vertebrates are often the primary consumers in plant communities (Paige and Whitham, 1987; Hodgson and Illius, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research on vertebrate herbivory.

claim: Vertebrate herbivores can exert strong selective pressure on plants by influencing growth, structural defenses, reproductive timing and mortality.
source: What we do know is that vertebrate herbivores can exert strong selective pressure on plants (Collins et al., 1998; Becerra, 2015) by influencing growth (Paige and Whitham, 1987; Bergman, 2002; Liu et al., 2012; Ishihama et al., 2014), structural defenses (Abrahamson, 1975; White, 1988; Young and Okello, 1998; Takada et al., 2001; Wilson and Kerley, 2003; Young et al., 2003; Kato et al., 2008), reproductive timing (Zamora et al., 2001) and mortality (Veblen et al., 1989; Gill, 1992; Vila and Guibal, 2001; Saint-Andrieux et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research on vertebrate herbivore effects on plants.

claim: Vertebrates tend to avoid plants that are rich in secondary metabolites, including condensed tannins and phenolics.
source: We also know that vertebrates tend to avoid plants that are rich in secondary metabolites, including condensed tannins and phenolics (Cooper and Owen-Smith, 1985; Owen Smith, 1993; Furstenburg and van Hoven, 1994; O'reilly-Wapstra et al., 2004; Jansen et al., 2007; DeGabriel et al., 2009; Rosenthal and Berenbaum, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research on vertebrate feeding preferences.

claim: Silencing the production of nicotine increases leaf damage by vertebrate browsers in the field.
source: Furthermore, it has been shown that silencing the production of the nervous toxin nicotine can engender increased leaf damage by vertebrate browsers in the field (Steppuhn et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research on nicotine-deficient plants.

claim: Three experimental N. attenuata populations were established in the Great Basin Desert, each consisting of a mix of jasmonate deficient and wild type plants.
source: To assess the importance of jasmonates in protecting plants from native arthropod and vertebrate herbivores, we studied three experimental N. attenuata populations in their native environment in the Great Basin Desert (United States). Each population consisted of a mix of jasmonate deficient and wild type plants.
evidence: Describes the experimental design of the field study.

claim: In the Lytle plot, jasmonate-deficient plants suffered more stem peeling and leaf removal by vertebrates, but similar arthropod damage compared to wild type plants.
source: In the Lytle plot, jasmonate-deficient plants suffered more stem peeling and leaf removal by vertebrates, but similar arthropod damage compared to wild type plants.
evidence: Supported by field observations and damage quantification in the Lytle plot.

claim: In the Lytle plot, jasmonate-deficient plants produced fewer flowers, and this effect was associated with higher occurrence of vertebrate stem peeling.
source: Jasmonate-deficient plants also produced fewer flowers. Likelihood ratio tests based on Generalized Linear Models (GLMs) showed that this effect was associated with the higher occurrence of vertebrate stem peeling in irAOC plants.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of field data from the Lytle plot.

claim: In the Snow plot, irAOC plants suffered more vertebrate leaf removal and damage from leaf chewing and leaf sucking/piercing insects than wild type plants.
source: In the Snow plot, irAOC plants suffered more vertebrate leaf removal and damage from leaf chewing and leaf sucking/piercing insects than the wild type plants, but only leaf removal by vertebrates was associated with a reduction in flower production.
evidence: Supported by field observations and damage quantification in the Snow plot.

claim: In the Snow plot, only leaf removal by vertebrates was associated with a reduction in flower production.
source: In the Snow plot, irAOC plants suffered more vertebrate leaf removal and damage from leaf chewing and leaf sucking/piercing insects than the wild type plants, but only leaf removal by vertebrates was associated with a reduction in flower production.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of field data from the Snow plot.

claim: In the Poplar plot, no vertebrate damage was observed.
source: In the Poplar plot, no vertebrate damage was observed, and jasmonate-deficiency increased damage by leaf sucking/piercing arthropods, but did not decrease flower production (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by field observations in the Poplar plot.

claim: In the Poplar plot, jasmonate-deficiency increased damage by leaf sucking/piercing arthropods, but did not decrease flower production.
source: In the Poplar plot, no vertebrate damage was observed, and jasmonate-deficiency increased damage by leaf sucking/piercing arthropods, but did not decrease flower production (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by field observations and statistical analysis in the Poplar plot.

claim: Jasmonate deficiency increased vertebrate damage more strongly than arthropod damage.
source: Overall, jasmonate deficiency increased vertebrate damage more strongly than arthropod damage, and only jasmonate-dependent changes in vertebrate damage translated into a decrease in flower production.
evidence: Supported by comparison of damage patterns across all three field plots.

claim: In wild type plants, wounding with Manduca sexta oral secretions did not significantly reduce peak flower production.
source: In wild type plants, W+OS induction did not significantly reduce peak flower production (Figure 2a).
evidence: Supported by glasshouse experiment data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Rosette defoliation reduced flower production by 24% in wild type plants.
source: All other treatments led to significant reductions in flower production: rosette defoliation reduced flower production by 24%, rosette and stem leaf removal reduced flower production by 53%, and stem peeling resulted in a marked 78% reduction in flower numbers.
evidence: Supported by glasshouse experiment data on simulated herbivory.

claim: Rosette and stem leaf removal reduced flower production by 53% in wild type plants.
source: All other treatments led to significant reductions in flower production: rosette defoliation reduced flower production by 24%, rosette and stem leaf removal reduced flower production by 53%, and stem peeling resulted in a marked 78% reduction in flower numbers.
evidence: Supported by glasshouse experiment data on simulated herbivory.

claim: Stem peeling resulted in a 78% reduction in flower numbers in wild type plants.
source: All other treatments led to significant reductions in flower production: rosette defoliation reduced flower production by 24%, rosette and stem leaf removal reduced flower production by 53%, and stem peeling resulted in a marked 78% reduction in flower numbers.
evidence: Supported by glasshouse experiment data on simulated herbivory.

claim: Full defoliation and stem peeling delayed the onset of flowering by more than two weeks.
source: Full defoliation and stem peeling also delayed the onset of flowering by more than two weeks.
evidence: Supported by glasshouse experiment data on flowering time.

claim: The total number of flowers was significantly higher in defoliated and stem-peeled irAOC plants than in similarly treated EV plants.
source: However, the total number of flowers was significantly higher in defoliated and stem-peeled irAOC plants than in similarly treated EV plants.
evidence: Supported by glasshouse experiment data comparing genotypes under defoliation treatments.

claim: Experimental stem peeling removed epidermis, cortex and phloem cells from the plant, leaving only xylem and pith cells.
source: Experimental stem peeling as a mimick of feeding patterns observed in the Lytle plot removed epidermis, cortex and phloem cells from the plant. The remaining tissue consisted of xylem and pith cells.
evidence: Supported by histological staining shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Simulated herbivory led to dramatic changes in both leaf and stem carbohydrate profiles and secondary metabolite levels in a jasmonate-dependent manner.
source: Redundancy analyses (RDAs) showed that simulated herbivory led to dramatic changes in both leaf- and stem carbohydrate profiles and secondary metabolite levels in a jasmonate-dependent manner (permutation test for the effect of the genotype x treatment interaction: p<0.001 in both tissues) (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by redundancy analysis of metabolite profiling data.

claim: Diterpene glycosides, rutin, nicotine, glucose and fructose in the leaves and nicotine, glucose and fructose in the stems explained most of the metabolic differences between induced EV and irAOC plants.
source: The RDAs further revealed that diterpene glycosides (DTGs), rutin, nicotine, glucose and fructose in the leaves and nicotine, glucose and fructose in the stems explained most of the metabolic differences between induced EV and irAOC plants (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by redundancy analysis identifying key metabolites with high correlation coefficients.

claim: Under control conditions, irAOC plants have lower nicotine and DTG concentrations in the leaves and lower nicotine levels in the stems than EV plants.
source: Closer inspection of these metabolites showed that under control conditions, irAOC plants have lower nicotine and DTG concentrations in the leaves and lower nicotine levels in the stems than EV plants.
evidence: Supported by metabolite profiling data comparing control plants of both genotypes.

claim: Upon induction, differences in nicotine and DTG concentrations between EV and irAOC plants became more pronounced.
source: Upon induction, these differences became even more pronounced (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by metabolite profiling data comparing induced plants of both genotypes.

claim: Constitutive rutin, glucose and fructose concentrations did not differ between genotypes, but were more strongly depleted in induced EV plants.
source: Constitutive rutin, glucose and fructose concentrations on the other hand did not differ between genotypes, but were more strongly depleted in induced EV plants (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by metabolite profiling data comparing control and induced plants.

claim: Cottontails rejected EV pellets and strongly preferred to feed from both irAOC pellets and pure alfalfa.
source: Comparisons of adjusted confidence intervals of asymptotes of logistic models fitted for each treatment showed that cottontails rejected EV pellets and strongly preferred to feed from both irAOC pellets and pure alfalfa (Figure 4a, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by feeding preference experiments with cottontail rabbits.

claim: Rabbits refused both nicotine complemented-irAOC and EV pellets and preferentially fed on alfalfa pellets.
source: Strikingly, rabbits refused both nicotine complemented-irAOC and EV pellets and preferentially fed on alfalfa pellets (Figure 4b).
evidence: Supported by nicotine complementation feeding experiments with cottontail rabbits.

claim: The drying process did not affect the water-loss corrected abundance of DTGs.
source: The drying process did not affect the water-loss corrected abundance of DTGs.
evidence: Supported by metabolite measurements before and after drying plant material.

claim: The abundances of nicotine, chlorogenic acid and rutin were reduced by drying, but jasmonate-dependent differences were conserved.
source: The abundances of nicotine, chlorogenic acid and rutin were reduced, but jasmonate-dependent differences were conserved.
evidence: Supported by metabolite measurements before and after drying plant material.

claim: The most abundant phenol amides dicaffeoylspermidine, dicoumarylspermidine, ferolylputrescine and caffeoylputrescine were degraded during the drying process, while less abundant phenol amides increased in concentration.
source: The most abundant phenol amides dicaffeoylspermidine, dicoumarylspermidine, ferolylputrescine and caffeoylputrescine were degraded during the drying process, while less abundant phenol amides increased in concentration.
evidence: Supported by metabolite measurements before and after drying plant material.

claim: Flower production in the absence of future damage is a valid and robust approximation for plant fitness in the predominantly self-pollinating N. attenuata.
source: Earlier studies demonstrate however that leaf damage at later developmental stages has little impact on plant fitness (Zavala and Baldwin, 2006) and that flower production in the absence of future damage is a valid and robust approximation for plant fitness in the predominantly self-pollinating N. attenuata (Baldwin et al., 1997; Baldwin, 2003; Hettenhausen et al., 2012; Schuman et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research on N. attenuata fitness measures.

claim: Vertebrate herbivores can have a profound impact on plant fitness and the distribution of plant species in nature.
source: Vertebrate herbivores can have a profound impact on plant fitness and the distribution of plant species in nature (Hulme, 1994; 1996; Shimoda et al., 1994; Palmisano and Fox, 1997; Waller and Alverson, 1997; Gómez and Zamora, 2000; Sessions and Kelly, 2001; Warner and Cushman, 2002; Maron and Crone, 2006; Maron and Kauffman, 2006; Nisi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research on vertebrate herbivore impacts.

claim: Paliurus ramosissimus trees that are intensively bark peeled by sika deer will take nearly 30 years to recover.
source: For instance, Paliurus ramosissimus trees that are intensively bark peeled by sika deer (Cervus nippon) will take nearly 30 years to recover (Ishihama et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research on bark peeling effects.

claim: Strong growth delays and increased tree mortality have been observed in other species following vertebrate herbivory.
source: Similarly, strong growth delays and increased tree mortality have been observed in other species (Veblen et al., 1989; Gill, 1992; Palmisano and Fox, 1997; Vila and Guibal, 2001; Saint-Andrieux et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research on vertebrate herbivore effects on trees.

claim: Vertebrate herbivores have rarely been considered in the context of plant defense signaling.
source: Surprisingly however, vertebrate herbivores have rarely been considered in the context of plant defense signaling (Dyer, 1980; Smith et al., 1991; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by review of literature on plant defense signaling research.

claim: Plant defense regulation has mostly been investigated in the context of arthropod herbivores and pathogens.
source: Instead, plant defense regulation has mostly been investigated in the context of arthropod herbivores and pathogens (Dixon et al., 1994; Chen et al., 1995; Yang et al., 1997; Rojo et al., 2003; Wu and Baldwin, 2009, Wu and Baldwin, 2010; Schmelz, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research on plant defense regulation.

claim: Arthropod damage in the field is generally low.
source: Although arthropod damage in the field is generally low (Steppuhn et al., 2004; Rayapuram and Baldwin, 2007; Pandey and Baldwin, 2008; Rayapuram et al., 2008; Johnson et al., 2009; Meldau et al., 2009; Stitz et al., 2011; Fischer et al., 2012; Kallenbach et al., 2012; Schuman et al., 2012; Schäfer et al., 2013), local outbreaks can lead to substantial plant damage (Van Bael et al., 1999; Cease et al., 2012; DeRose and Long, 2012; Ðinh et al., 2013), and several studies show that arthropods influence plant fitness (Baldwin, 1998; Maron, 1998; Kessler and Baldwin, 2004; Machado et al., 2013) and may drive the evolution of plant defenses (Huber et al., 2016; Poelman and Kessler, 2016; Züst and Agrawal, 2016) including plant defense signaling (Durrant et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2015a).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous field studies on arthropod damage.

claim: Local outbreaks of arthropods can lead to substantial plant damage.
source: Although arthropod damage in the field is generally low (Steppuhn et al., 2004; Rayapuram and Baldwin, 2007; Pandey and Baldwin, 2008; Rayapuram et al., 2008; Johnson et al., 2009; Meldau et al., 2009; Stitz et al., 2011; Fischer et al., 2012; Kallenbach et al., 2012; Schuman et al., 2012; Schäfer et al., 2013), local outbreaks can lead to substantial plant damage (Van Bael et al., 1999; Cease et al., 2012; DeRose and Long, 2012; Ðinh et al., 2013), and several studies show that arthropods influence plant fitness (Baldwin, 1998; Maron, 1998; Kessler and Baldwin, 2004; Machado et al., 2013) and may drive the evolution of plant defenses (Huber et al., 2016; Poelman and Kessler, 2016; Züst and Agrawal, 2016) including plant defense signaling (Durrant et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2015a).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research on arthropod outbreaks.

claim: Arthropods influence plant fitness and may drive the evolution of plant defenses including plant defense signaling.
source: Although arthropod damage in the field is generally low (Steppuhn et al., 2004; Rayapuram and Baldwin, 2007; Pandey and Baldwin, 2008; Rayapuram et al., 2008; Johnson et al., 2009; Meldau et al., 2009; Stitz et al., 2011; Fischer et al., 2012; Kallenbach et al., 2012; Schuman et al., 2012; Schäfer et al., 2013), local outbreaks can lead to substantial plant damage (Van Bael et al., 1999; Cease et al., 2012; DeRose and Long, 2012; Ðinh et al., 2013), and several studies show that arthropods influence plant fitness (Baldwin, 1998; Maron, 1998; Kessler and Baldwin, 2004; Machado et al., 2013) and may drive the evolution of plant defenses (Huber et al., 2016; Poelman and Kessler, 2016; Züst and Agrawal, 2016) including plant defense signaling (Durrant et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2015a).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research on arthropod effects on plant fitness and defense evolution.

claim: It is crucial to include both arthropod and vertebrate herbivores when studying the ecology and evolution of plant defense regulation.
source: Given the context-dependent potential of both arthropod and vertebrate herbivores to act as agents of natural selection, it seems crucial to include both groups when studying the ecology and evolution of plant defense regulation (Strauss, 1991; Hulme, 1994; 1996; Palmisano and Fox, 1997; Sessions and Kelly, 2001; Oduor et al., 2010).
evidence: Based on inference from the context-dependent effects of both herbivore types and citations to previous research.

claim: Plant secondary metabolites can influence vertebrate foraging patterns.
source: Numerous studies have found that plant secondary metabolites can influence vertebrate foraging patterns (Freeland and Janzen, 1974; McArthur et al., 1995; Mithen et al., 1995; Dearing et al., 2005; Scogings et al., 2011; Mkhize et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research on secondary metabolites and vertebrate feeding.

claim: Vertebrates tend to avoid plants that are rich in condensed tannins, phenolics and alkaloids.
source: Vertebrates tend to avoid plants that are rich in condensed tannins, phenolics and alkaloids (Cooper and Owen-Smith, 1985; Owen Smith, 1993; Furstenburg and van Hoven, 1994; O'reilly-Wapstra et al., 2004; Jansen et al., 2007; Steppuhn et al., 2008; DeGabriel et al., 2009; Rosenthal and Berenbaum, 2012): Quinolizidine alkaloids for instance seem to protect lupin (Lupinus spp) plants from rabbits (Oryctolagus spp.) (Wink, 1985; 1988; Fattorusso and Taglialatela-Scafati, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research on vertebrate avoidance of toxic plants.

claim: Quinolizidine alkaloids protect lupin plants from rabbits.
source: Vertebrates tend to avoid plants that are rich in condensed tannins, phenolics and alkaloids (Cooper and Owen-Smith, 1985; Owen Smith, 1993; Furstenburg and van Hoven, 1994; O'reilly-Wapstra et al., 2004; Jansen et al., 2007; Steppuhn et al., 2008; DeGabriel et al., 2009; Rosenthal and Berenbaum, 2012): Quinolizidine alkaloids for instance seem to protect lupin (Lupinus spp) plants from rabbits (Oryctolagus spp.) (Wink, 1985; 1988; Fattorusso and Taglialatela-Scafati, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research on quinolizidine alkaloids.

claim: Primary metabolites such as carbohydrates can affect mammalian feeding preferences.
source: However, apart from toxic secondary metabolites, primary metabolites such as carbohydrates can also affect mammalian feeding preferences (Mayland et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research on carbohydrates and feeding preferences.

claim: Leaves and stems of jasmonate-deficient plants consistently contained lower levels of nicotine and higher levels of glucose and fructose compared to wild type plants.
source: In this study, leaves and stems of jasmonate-deficient plants consistently contained lower levels of nicotine and higher levels of glucose and fructose compared to wild type plants.
evidence: Supported by metabolite profiling data from glasshouse experiments.

claim: The amount of nicotine produced via jasmonate signaling is sufficient to dictate cottontail feeding preferences.
source: This finding suggests that the amount of nicotine produced via jasmonate signaling is sufficient to dictate cottontail feeding preferences.
evidence: Based on inference from nicotine complementation experiments showing restored avoidance.

claim: The increased damage and reduced flower production in jasmonate-deficient plants in the field can be attributed to reduced nicotine concentrations.
source: They further suggest that the increased damage and reduced flower production in jasmonate-deficient plants in the field can be attributed to reduced nicotine concentrations.
evidence: Based on inference from feeding experiments and field observations.

claim: Nicotine is a nervous system toxin that can bind to acetylcholine receptors of synaptic cells leading to neuromuscular blockade.
source: Nicotine is a nervous system toxin that can bind to acetylcholine receptors of synaptic cells leading to neuromuscular blockade (Albuquerque et al., 2009; Prochaska and Benowitz, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research on nicotine toxicity.

claim: The median lethal dose (LD50) of nicotine varies between 3–50 mg*kg-1 for small rodents.
source: Its median lethal dose (LD50) varies between 3–50 mg*kg-1 for small rodents (Wink, 1993; Karačonji, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research on nicotine toxicity in rodents.

claim: Nicotine is produced at concentrations of up to 3 mg*g FW-1 in N. attenuata shoots.
source: As nicotine is produced at concentrations of up to 3 mg*g FW-1 in N. attenuata shoots, the consumption of a single wild-type plant can be lethal to a small vertebrate herbivore.
evidence: Supported by metabolite measurements in N. attenuata shoots.

claim: The consumption of a single wild-type N. attenuata plant can be lethal to a small vertebrate herbivore.
source: As nicotine is produced at concentrations of up to 3 mg*g FW-1 in N. attenuata shoots, the consumption of a single wild-type plant can be lethal to a small vertebrate herbivore.
evidence: Based on inference from nicotine concentration data and LD50 values.

claim: The desert woodrat (Neotoma lepida) may excise N. attenuata leaves, dry them and transfer them to their nests.
source: Interestingly, certain vertebrates such as the desert woodrat (Neotoma lepida) seem to excise N. attenuata leaves, dry them and transfer them to their nests (Baldwin, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous observation of woodrat behavior.

claim: It has been proposed that woodrat behavior of collecting N. attenuata leaves may allow woodrats to use nicotine as pharmaceutical means to reduce ectoparasite loads.
source: It has been proposed that this behavior may allow woodrats to use nicotine as pharmaceutical means to reduce ectoparasite loads (Baldwin, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous speculation about woodrat behavior.

claim: The irAOC line has herbivory-induced jasmonate levels reduced by more than 95%.
source: The irAOC line has been characterized previously (Kallenbach et al., 2012). Its herbivory-induced jasmonate levels are reduced by more than 95% (Kallenbach et al., 2012; Machado et al., 2013) while flower production is similar to WT plants in the absence of herbivore attack (Machado et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous characterization of the irAOC line.

claim: The irAOC line has flower production similar to WT plants in the absence of herbivore attack.
source: The irAOC line has been characterized previously (Kallenbach et al., 2012). Its herbivory-induced jasmonate levels are reduced by more than 95% (Kallenbach et al., 2012; Machado et al., 2013) while flower production is similar to WT plants in the absence of herbivore attack (Machado et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous characterization of the irAOC line.

claim: Four main herbivore damage types were observed across all three plots: leaf removal, stem peeling, leaf chewing and leaf sucking/piercing.
source: Across all three plots, we observed four main herbivore damage types: leaf removal, stem peeling, leaf chewing and leaf sucking/piercing.
evidence: Supported by field observations and damage classification.

claim: The different damage types are characteristic for different herbivores including deer, rabbits, wood rats, gophers, caterpillars, ants, mirid bugs and leafhoppers.
